lead: Ripple, Quorum, Tendermint, Kadena and Rootstock answer five needs: fast payment settlement, private smart contracts, immediate BFT finality, parallel-chain scalability and Bitcoin compatibility. Only a few universities teach this set. Each is a design choice. Ripple settles cross-border payments, Quorum hides enterprise transactions, Tendermint commits in one BFT round of prevote and precommit, Kadena braids proof-of-work chains, and Rootstock brings Ethereum contracts to Bitcoin.
prereq: You need Unit 3 consensus and Unit 5 EVM and smart contracts; see 6.8 for the limits these designs face.

sections.h3: Ripple and Quorum: settlement and privacy

blocks.text: Ripple is a payment network; the XRP Ledger is its public ledger. Validators agree using a trusted list, often called the unique node list. There is no mining race. A payment can settle in seconds, and the ledger carries XRP or issued balances such as dollars or rupees. Banks use this model for cross-border settlement, where correspondent banking is slow and costly. Settlement happens on the ledger itself, not in a smart contract; the ledger records balances and payments.

Quorum is permissioned Ethereum for enterprises. It keeps the EVM and Solidity, so Ethereum contracts move across. Known nodes are admitted by a consortium. Private transactions send the payload only to selected nodes; other nodes see that a private transaction happened, not its contents. Consensus can be Raft for crash faults or IBFT/QBFT for Byzantine faults. A bank consortium shares one state without exposing every trade to every member. This is useful for trade finance.

Tendermint is Byzantine fault tolerant consensus. Validators take turns proposing a block, then prevote and precommit. A block commits when more than two-thirds of voting power signs the same precommit. Finality is immediate: after commit it does not roll back under the fault assumption. Each Cosmos chain runs Tendermint-style consensus, and the IBC protocol links these chains.

For n validators with equal voting power, a block needs more than two-thirds of voting power. In votes, quorum = floor(2n/3) + 1. This equals 2f + 1 only when n = 3f + 1, where f = floor((n − 1) / 3) is the maximum number of faulty validators the network can tolerate. With n = 7, f = floor(6 / 3) = 2, and quorum = floor(14 / 3) + 1 = 4 + 1 = 5. Five matching votes commit; four do not. Bitcoin's longest-chain rule is probabilistic; a Tendermint commit is a fixed decision.

Kadena uses Chainweb, a braid of parallel proof-of-work chains. Each chain mines its own blocks and includes headers from peer chains, so work on one chain strengthens others. More chains raise throughput. Pact is Kadena's smart-contract language, built for readable contracts and formal checks. The trade is complexity: users must track many chains and cross-chain proofs.

Rootstock is a Bitcoin sidechain with an EVM. It is merge-mined with Bitcoin, so miners reuse hash power. A peg backs RBTC with BTC. A user moves BTC in, runs Solidity contracts, and moves value back through the peg. Bitcoin holders gain smart contracts without changing Bitcoin's base rules. The peg is run by a federation, so trust is not identical to Bitcoin's.

blocks.text: The table is the exam map: settlement, privacy, finality, scalability and compatibility are separate axes. Strength on one axis does not imply strength on another. Quorum is permissioned for participation. The XRP Ledger is a public ledger anyone can use, but its validators are chosen through a trusted unique node list published by Ripple, so validation is permissioned while participation is open. Tendermint's validator set is fixed by the app: often permissioned, but public on stake-based chains. Kadena and Rootstock are public.

figure.caption: Five of the seven validators sign the same precommit, so the block commits; four would not be enough. The two validators who do not sign are exactly the f = 2 faults the network can tolerate.

examples.question: A Tendermint network has 7 validators with equal voting power. Find f and the quorum. How many votes commit a block?
steps: f = floor((n − 1) / 3) = floor(6 / 3) = 2, so the network tolerates at most 2 faulty validators.
5 of 7 votes is more than two-thirds; 4 of 7 is not.
examples.answer: f = 2 is the maximum number of faulty validators tolerated; the quorum is 5 votes, so 5 matching votes commit the block.

f = (n - 1) // 3

traps: Tendermint's threshold is voting power, not node count; with equal validators they match.
XRP is a token on the XRP Ledger; Ripple is the company and payment network.
Quorum private data is hidden from non-participants, not from participants or transaction metadata.
Kadena's braid is many proof-of-work chains, not one sharded chain.
Rootstock is a sidechain with a peg, not a Bitcoin soft fork.

quiz.a: Byzantine fault tolerant voting with proposer rounds.

quiz.q: What is the XRP Ledger validator list?
quiz.a: The trusted set whose agreement settles transactions.

quiz.q: Why does Quorum keep the EVM?
quiz.a: So existing Solidity contracts and tools work in a permissioned network.

quiz.q: For n = 10 equal validators, compute f and quorum.
Compare finality in Tendermint and Bitcoin.
quiz.a: Tendermint commits after more than two-thirds precommit and is final; Bitcoin is probabilistic and can reorganise.

quiz.q: Why is Rootstock a sidechain rather than a Bitcoin fork?
quiz.a: It runs separately and pegs BTC, so Bitcoin's base rules stay unchanged.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry work continues on payment corridors, privacy-preserving EVM chains, Cosmos interchain security, Chainweb cross-chain transfers and Bitcoin sidechain pegs. Search for RippleNet, Quorum Tessera, CometBFT, Chainweb, Pact and Rootstock RBTC. Read their consensus and peg assumptions before comparing throughput.
